data.title: Starý Koňuš – a Bronze Age hillfort on a table mountain
data.excerpt: A table mountain in the cadastral area of the village of Koňuš in eastern Slovakia, once called Stari Konjus, carries a massive hillfort and hilltop settlement of the Bronze Age that the Slavs later used as well. Its rampart reaches up to 8 m on the more accessible western side, and the literature gives the area of the hillfort as 7.8 ha.
data.metaTitle: Starý Koňuš – a Bronze Age hillfort on a table mountain
data.metaDescription: On a table mountain above Koňuš stood a massive hillfort of 7.8 ha with a rampart up to 8 m high, later used by the Slavs in the 10th–11th centuries.

keyFacts.label: Height of the rampart defences
keyFacts.value: up to 8 m on the western (more accessible) side, 1–3 m on the other sides

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Popričný vrch, east of the village of Koňuš, Michalovce district

keyFacts.label: Slavic finds
keyFacts.value: 8 pottery fragments dated to the 10th – 11th centuries

keyFacts.label: Water source
keyFacts.value: a spring on the slope of the hillfort, which did not dry up even in the drought

timeline.title: The arrival of the Gáva culture
timeline.description: In eastern Slovakia the Gáva culture replaced the Piliny culture and the Suciu de Sus culture and became the bearer of the most intensive occupation of the hillfort in the later part of the Late Bronze Age.

timeline.title: The end of the Bronze Age occupation
timeline.description: Occupation by the bearers of the Gáva culture lasted on the hillfort until the end of the Bronze Age.

timeline.title: Slavic occupation of the hillfort
timeline.description: The eight pottery fragments found here can be dated to this period, that is, to the period of the decline of Great Moravia and the subsequent unstable formation of the Hungarian state; the hillfort perhaps offered the Slavs a refuge from the pressure of the Old Hungarian tribal warbands into the Medzibodrožie region.

timeline.title: Archaeological excavation of the hillfort
timeline.description: The excavation of the hillfort was carried out back in the 1950s.

mediaTexts.caption: A view of the “Starý Koňuš” enclosure from the west; the steep slopes of the upland plateau stand out better this way. The green marks are the access paths, the red ones are clearly visible ramparts (NW or SE) or (on the least steep W side) high terraces with steep slopes below them. The blue one is the spring that did not dry up despite the drought. At the eastern end the plateau narrows into a thin ridge, which was protected by a high rampart, today partly damaged by the road. It is wonderfully peaceful there, come for a walk.

mediaTexts.caption: The sloping plain in the western part of the hillfort enclosure lies on a terrace; to the right (no longer visible) is a steep break of slope. The vegetation made it impossible to photograph. This is the least protected stretch, which is why the ramparts here should be up to 8 m high. There were no ramparts, but in places the terrace is more than 8 m higher (perhaps even 20).

children.text: In the cadastral area of the village of Koňuš (Michalovce district) in eastern Slovakia, a massive hillfort and hilltop settlement of the Bronze Age, later used by the Slavs as well, rises on a high hill – a table mountain once called Stari Konjus. According to the literature the area of the hillfort is 7.8 ha. It will, however, have to be surveyed again. The rampart defences on the more accessible western side reach a height of up to 8 m, the other sides from 1 to 3 m. Who knows when the Slavs moved down to the foot of the mountain and founded the new village of Koňuš… they still use the meadows, though. The excavation of the hillfort was carried out back in the 1950s.
Hradisko Starý Koňuš - národna kultúrna pamiatka

The site occupies a long meadow on the upland plateau of the hill, in the western part of the Popričný vrch massif, east of the village of Koňuš. It is best reached from the valley of the Syrový potok stream. The meadow mentioned slopes gently from E to W. Its western end is closed by a stone rampart, cut through by a mountain road.

children.text: Numerous finds of sherds from the survey (mostly non-diagnostic) suggest that the site was most intensively occupied in the later part of that period, probably by the Gáva culture, which in eastern Slovakia replaced the Piliny culture and the Suciu de Sus culture around 1200 BC. It lasted here until the end of the Bronze Age – until 750 BC. This period is characterised by the building of hillforts, distinctive pottery and extensive bronze metallurgy (jewellery, weapons, body armour, helmets, drinking sets, vessels).

Bowl-shaped vessels are represented on the hillfort by a fragment of a hemispherical vessel with a slightly thickened and gently everted rim, a sherd of a thin-walled vessel with a carination in the upper part of the body and several fragments of conical bowls with the mouth thickened on the inside. The fragments mentioned come from vessels brown or brownish-grey on the outside and blackish-grey on the inside. Vase-shaped vessels are attested by a fragment with a horizontal relief rib and by a sherd decorated with bundles of grooves, both blackish-grey on the outside and brown on the inside. The most numerous pieces in the pottery material are fragments of pot-shaped vessels with a straight or slightly curved neck, mostly brown.

The blue one is the spring that did not dry up despite the drought. At the eastern end the plateau narrows into a thin ridge, which was protected by a high rampart, today partly damaged by the road. children.text: Budinský-Krička states that, judging by the finds, the plateau of the hill was probably sought out only sporadically in this period. The Slavs could have used the hillfort as a refuge, but Krička also points out the strategic importance of this site, which lies above the road between the region below Vihorlat and the basin of the Uh in the territory of present-day Ukraine. The eight pottery fragments found (the more diagnostic among them being a dark grey sherd decorated with a row of stab impressions and a wavy line, a reddish-brown fragment with decoration of horizontal grooves and a brownish-grey fragment with traces of horizontal flutes) can be dated to the 10th or 11th century, that is, to the period of the decline of Great Moravia and the subsequent unstable period of the formation of the Hungarian state. The hillfort perhaps offered the Slavs a refuge from the pressure of the Old Hungarian tribal warbands into the Medzibodrožie region.
